What is REST? What are its constraints?

REST (REpresentational State Transfer) is an architectural style built on HTTP. Its constraints: client–server, stateless (each request carries everything needed), cacheable, uniform interface (resources identified by URIs, manipulated through representations, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS), layered system, and optionally code-on-demand.
REST vs SOAP vs GraphQL vs gRPC?

REST | SOAP | GraphQL | gRPC
Style over HTTP; JSON | Protocol; XML envelope, WSDL | One endpoint; the client picks its fields | HTTP/2 + Protobuf, binary, streaming
Simple, cacheable | WS-Security, strict contracts | No over- or under-fetching | Very fast service-to-service calls
What does idempotent mean? Is PUT idempotent? POST?

Idempotent means repeating the same request N times has the same effect as sending it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS are idempotent. POST isn't: two POSTs create two orders. To make a POST safe to retry, have the client send an Idempotency-Key header and have the server store and deduplicate it.
PUT vs PATCH vs POST?

PUT replaces the entire resource at a known URI; fields you leave out are reset. PATCH changes only the fields you send (JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch). POST creates a resource under a collection, where the server assigns the id, or runs a non-CRUD action.
401 Unauthorized: you aren't authenticated (the token is missing or invalid). Send credentials. 403 Forbidden: you're authenticated but don't have permission (wrong role).
Best practices for URI design?

- Use nouns, plural, lowercase, hyphenated: /api/v1/order-items
- Express hierarchy with paths: /customers/42/orders
- Put filtering, sorting and paging in the query: ?status=PAID&sort=createdAt,desc&page=0&size=20
- No verbs in URIs; the HTTP method is the verb. Use action sub-resources only for real actions: POST /orders/7/cancel
- Return a consistent error body (RFC 9457 ProblemDetail).
How do you version an API?

URI versioning (/v1/users, the most common), a header (X-API-Version: 2), media type (Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json), or a query param (?version=2). Never break existing clients. Add fields compatibly and deprecate old versions with a sunset date.
How do you implement pagination?

Offset (page/size, Spring Pageable): simple, but slow for deep pages and unstable when rows are inserted. Cursor/keyset (?after=lastId, WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT n): fast and stable, good for infinite scroll. Return metadata (totalElements, next link).
What is HATEOAS?

Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State: responses include links to the actions available next (_links: { self, cancel, pay }), so the client discovers the flow instead of hard-coding URLs. Spring HATEOAS provides EntityModel and linkTo(methodOn(...)).
How do you secure a REST API?

HTTPS everywhere · authentication (OAuth2 / JWT / API keys) · role- or scope-based authorization · input validation · rate limiting (429) · proper CORS · don't leak stack traces · hash passwords with BCrypt · protect against injection (parameterized queries) · audit logging · short-lived tokens with refresh.
What is CORS?

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the browser hides the response of a JS call to a different origin (the simple request is still sent) unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Non-simple requests (PUT, custom headers, JSON) are preceded by an OPTIONS preflight. In Spring, use @CrossOrigin or a global CorsConfigurationSource plus http.cors().
How do you document APIs?

OpenAPI 3 / Swagger: add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui and you get /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs. Annotate with @Operation, @ApiResponse, @Schema. Contract-first teams generate code from the YAML spec instead.
How do you use HTTP caching in REST?
Use Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag with If-None-Match (returns 304 if unchanged), and Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since. Spring offers ShallowEtagHeaderFilter and ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(..).
Is REST the same as HTTP? Can you have REST without HTTP?

No. REST is an architectural style, and HTTP is a protocol. Fielding's constraints do not mention HTTP, though it was designed alongside them, and is the only common implementation. Likewise, using HTTP does not make an API RESTful: a single POST endpoint uses HTTP but is at level 0.
What does stateless really mean? Does it forbid a database or login?

It means the server keeps no client session state between requests; each request supplies what is needed, such as a token. Resource state in a database is normal. A server-side session is a departure from the constraint, but a Redis-backed session still gives many of the scaling benefits. A login that issues a token fits well.
What is the Richardson Maturity Model? Where do most APIs sit?

Level 0 is one endpoint. Level 1 adds resources. Level 2 adds HTTP verbs and status codes. Level 3 adds hypermedia. Most production APIs are at level 2, because level 3's cost rarely pays off for internal clients. Fielding says only level 3 is truly REST.
Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?

Yes. Idempotency concerns the effect on server state, and not the response. After one or many calls, the resource is gone. Returning 204 on all calls is also valid. What matters is that a retried delete does no extra harm.
Is PATCH idempotent? Is POST ever idempotent?

PATCH is not guaranteed. It depends on the document: "set status" is, "append item" is not. POST is not by definition, but an idempotency key or natural unique key can make a specific endpoint behave idempotently.
Why are safe and idempotent methods important in practice?

Intermediaries and clients act on them. Browsers and proxies can retry a GET; HTTP clients automatically retry idempotent requests on connection failure; crawlers and link previewers fetch GET links. An unsafe action behind a GET, such as GET /logout, can be triggered accidentally, and enables CSRF.
PUT vs POST for creation: when does each apply?

POST to a collection when the server chooses the identifier. PUT when the client knows the URI, as with PUT /users/alice/settings, or a client-generated UUID, which makes creation naturally idempotent. PUT returns 201 on create, and 200 or 204 on replace.
What is the difference between 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308?

301 and 308 are permanent, and 302, 303 and 307 are temporary. 301 and 302 allow clients to change POST to GET, for historical reasons. 307 and 308 forbid that. 303 explicitly tells the client to GET another URI, which fits the Post/Redirect/Get pattern and finished async jobs.
A validation failure: 400 or 422? A duplicate email: 400 or 409?

Validation is either 400 or 422, chosen consistently; Spring's default is 400. A duplicate email is usually 409, since the request is valid but conflicts with existing state. Be aware that it confirms that the email exists; a registration flow may respond generically to prevent account enumeration.

All usually come from a gateway. 502: the upstream sent an invalid response, or the connection dropped, as in a crash. 503: the service is unavailable, for example no healthy instances, or overload. 504: the upstream took too long. Diagnosis differs: crashed pods, capacity, or slow dependencies.
Should a client receive 404 or 403 for someone else's resource?

404 is generally better for object-level access, as 403 confirms existence, which helps enumeration. 403 suits role-based denial on a route everyone knows about. Be consistent, and log the real reason.
Offset vs keyset pagination: explain why OFFSET 1000000 is slow.

The database cannot jump to a row number; it must walk and discard the first million index entries or rows, so cost grows with depth. Keyset uses an indexed WHERE condition to seek directly, so cost is stable at any depth. It cannot jump to arbitrary pages, and needs a unique sort key.
Why use an opaque cursor rather than exposing lastId?

An opaque cursor hides the implementation, letting the server change the sort or storage without an API break, and it can hold several fields such as a timestamp and id. Clients cannot craft positions, particularly if the cursor is signed. It also tells clients not to do arithmetic on it.
What is the right way to return a paginated Spring Data Page?

Returning PageImpl directly serializes an internal structure that may change; Spring Data warns about this. Map it to your own response record, or use PagedModel, or @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO). A stable shape is part of your API contract.
How would you evolve a response field from a string to an object without breaking clients?

Do not change it in place. Add a new field, such as shippingAddress next to address, and keep the old one populated. Mark it deprecated in the OpenAPI document, track its usage, notify consumers, and remove it after a sunset date, or in a new version. Consumer-driven contract tests help detect dependants.
What is a breaking change? Is adding an enum value one?

It is any change that can fail a correct existing client: removing fields, changing types, adding required inputs, or stricter validation. Adding an enum value is technically additive, but breaks clients that deserialize strictly, which Jackson does by default. So document the rule, and have clients use READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL or a default.
no-cache vs no-store?
A common confusion. no-cache permits storing, but requires revalidation before use, so you get cheap 304s. no-store forbids storing anywhere, for sensitive data.
How do ETags prevent the lost update problem?

Two clients read version 3. Client A sends PUT with If-Match: "3", and it succeeds, making version 4. Client B sends If-Match: "3", and gets 412, so it must re-read and merge. This is optimistic concurrency over HTTP. On the server, combine it with JPA's @Version, which closes the small gap between check and write.
Walk through implementing an idempotency key. What are the race conditions?

Two concurrent duplicates must not both proceed, so a unique constraint on the key picks one winner; a check-then-insert is a race. The loser returns 409, or waits for the result. If the worker crashes after charging but before recording, the record remains in progress, so you need a timeout, plus a downstream call that also carries the key. Hash the request, to detect a key reused with different content.
Which errors should be stored against an idempotency key?

Store definitive outcomes, including business 4xx responses, so that a retry gets the same answer. Do not store transient failures such as 5xx or timeouts where nothing happened, so that the retry can really try again. Validation failures that happen before work begins need not be stored at all.
Why does RFC 9457 matter? How would you handle a mix of error types?

A standard shape lets gateways, libraries and clients handle errors generally, without a custom parser per API. Keep type stable, extend with fields like errors, and localize title and detail, if needed. Make filter-level errors such as 401 and 429 use the same format, or clients must handle two.
Implement a rate limit across 10 instances. What are the challenges?

A shared store is needed, usually Redis. The token-bucket check must be atomic, so use a Lua script, or Bucket4j's Redis integration. Each check adds latency, so a small local allocation can reduce that, at some accuracy cost. Clock differences are avoided by using Redis time. Define behaviour for when Redis fails, and use per-tenant keys, so one customer cannot exhaust others' capacity.
Client sends 10,000 items in one POST. How do you design this?

Set a limit and reject above it with 413. For large volumes, accept a file or stream, return 202 with a job, and process in chunks of committed batches. Report per-item results, and make it resumable through per-item idempotency. For medium sizes, use synchronous partial success with 207.
Long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket vs webhooks?

Technique | Direction | Fit
Polling | Client asks | Simple, infrequent
Long polling | Server holds the request | Works anywhere; heavy
SSE | Server to browser over HTTP | Notifications, progress; reconnects automatically
WebSocket | Two-way | Chat, collaboration
Webhooks | Server to server | Integrations
Why compute a webhook signature over raw bytes, and why compare in constant time?

Parsing and re-serializing JSON can change whitespace or key order, breaking the HMAC, so verify the exact bytes received. String.equals exits at the first differing byte, leaking timing information that may help forge a signature; MessageDigest.isEqual avoids that. A timestamp in the signed data stops replay of an old capture.
When is GraphQL a poor choice?

When an API is simple CRUD with stable consumers, when CDN caching is important, when file transfer dominates, or for service-to-service calls. Adopting it means handling query cost limits, N+1, authorization per field, and non-HTTP-based error monitoring. It pays off with many diverse clients on a rich data graph.
Why is gRPC faster than JSON over HTTP?

Protobuf is compact and parses quickly, without field names on the wire. HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection, with header compression. Generated stubs also save hand-written code. The gain is real for high-volume internal traffic, and modest when a slow database dominates. HTTP/2 support is possible for REST, too, so the protocol alone is not the difference.
How do you make a client resilient when calling your REST API?

Set connect and read timeouts. Retry only idempotent operations, or those with a key, with exponential backoff and jitter, and honour Retry-After. Add a circuit breaker such as Resilience4j. Limit concurrency with a bulkhead. Handle unknown fields and enum values gracefully, and propagate a deadline across calls where possible.
How do you ensure the API contract stays stable between teams?

Keep the OpenAPI document in version control, generate or verify from it, diff in CI to catch breaking changes, and add consumer-driven contract tests such as Pact or Spring Cloud Contract. Have a deprecation policy with sunset dates, and monitor who still uses old fields or versions.
Design: a REST API for a payment system.

- Resources: /payments, /payments/{id}/refunds, with a state machine: CREATED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED, FAILED.
- Idempotency: a mandatory key on POST, forwarded to the provider.
- Amounts: integer minor units with an ISO 4217 currency.
- Async: 202 for slow providers, plus a signed webhook for results.
- Consistency: an outbox for events, a ledger with append-only entries, and If-Match on changes.
- Security: OAuth2 scopes, per-object authorization, TLS, and no raw card data.
- Errors: RFC 9457 with decline codes.
- Operations: per-merchant rate limits, audit logs, and trace ids.
How do you design a file upload API safely?

Accept multipart/form-data, or a presigned URL flow for large files. Enforce size limits in both the proxy and the app. Detect the real type from the content rather than the extension or the client header, and keep an allow-list of types. Store the file under a generated name outside the web root, never under the user's path, to prevent path traversal. Scan for malware where required, and serve files back with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so that an uploaded HTML file cannot run as a page on your domain. Return 201 with the new resource's location, and 413 or 415 for files that are too big or of the wrong type.
How do you return a download with a non-ASCII file name, such as an invoice in Tamil or with accents?

Use the RFC 6266 / RFC 5987 form filename*=UTF-8''... (percent-encoded), which Spring's ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) produces. Building the header by string concatenation breaks on quotes and non-ASCII characters, and can allow header injection. On the Angular side, read the name from the header. With CORS, the server must list Content-Disposition in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, or the browser hides it from JavaScript.
Soft delete: what should GET return after a resource is deleted?

To the API client, a soft-deleted resource should look deleted. DELETE returns 204. A later GET returns 404, or 410 Gone if you want to say that it existed and was removed on purpose. List endpoints leave it out. If users can restore items, model that explicitly, for example POST /documents/7/restore or a /trash collection. Watch for unique constraints, such as a deleted user's email blocking a new signup. Also, soft delete alone does not satisfy "right to erasure" requirements for personal data.
What is a correlation id, and how is it different from a trace id?

A correlation or request id is a single value attached to every log line and response for one request, often X-Request-Id. A trace id (W3C traceparent) does the same job, and also carries span ids, so tracing tools can show the timing tree across services. With Micrometer Tracing, use the trace id as your correlation id: it is already in the MDC, so log it and return it to clients. A separate request id is useful mainly when there is no tracing, or for an id the client creates and controls.
The Angular screen makes 12 API calls to render one page. How do you fix a chatty API?

Options: embed related data on request (GET /orders/7?expand=customer,items, as Stripe does). Add a purpose-built read endpoint or a BFF (Backend for Frontend) that aggregates calls on the server, close to the data. Use field selection to keep payloads small. Use GraphQL if many different screens need flexible shapes. Also check that the calls run in parallel (forkJoin) rather than in sequence, and that HTTP/2 is enabled. Keep the core resources clean, and put the aggregation in the BFF layer.
Should a REST API reject unknown fields in a request body?

The usual rule is the tolerant reader: ignore unknown fields, which is Spring Boot's Jackson default. This lets clients and servers evolve independently. A newer client can send a field that an older server does not know yet, and nothing breaks. The trade-off is that typos are silently ignored, so validate required fields explicitly. Some teams reject unknown fields on PATCH or other critical commands, where a misspelled field would silently do nothing. In that case, document it, and return 400 with the name of the unknown field.
Path variable vs query parameter vs header vs body: where does a value belong?

| Path variable | Query parameter | Header | Body
Use for | Identifying a resource | Filtering, sorting, paging | Metadata: auth, content type, idempotency key | The representation being created or changed
Example | /patients/42 | ?status=OPEN&page=2 | Authorization, If-Match | JSON of the new order
Optional? | No | Usually | Depends | Required for POST/PUT
Logged in URLs | Yes | Yes | Usually not | No
Spring | @PathVariable | @RequestParam | @RequestHeader | @RequestBody
Rule of thumb: if removing the value changes which resource you mean, it goes in the path; if it narrows a collection, it is a query parameter. Never put tokens or personal data in either, because URLs end up in logs and browser history.
200 vs 201 vs 202 vs 204: which success code for a write?

Code | Meaning | Body | Typical endpoint
200 OK | Done, here is the result | Yes | PUT or PATCH returning the updated resource
201 Created | A new resource exists | Optional, plus a Location header | POST /orders
202 Accepted | Queued, not done yet | A status link to poll | Report generation, bulk import
204 No Content | Done, nothing to return | Must be empty | DELETE, or PUT without a response body
URI location = uriBuilder.path("/orders/{id}").buildAndExpand(saved.id()).toUri();
return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved);
Rule of thumb: 201 with Location for creation, 202 when the work finishes later, 204 when there is nothing useful to send back. Returning 200 for everything works but hides information clients can use.
JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch vs a partial DTO: how do you implement PATCH?

| JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) | JSON Patch (RFC 6902) | Partial DTO
Content type | application/merge-patch+json | application/json-patch+json | application/json
Body | An object with only the changed fields | A list of operations: add, remove, replace, move, copy, test | DTO with nullable fields
Set a field to null | null means remove | replace with null or remove | Ambiguous: missing or null?
Arrays | Replaced whole | Element-level changes | Replaced whole
Client effort | Low | Higher | Low
Rule of thumb: merge patch fits most form edits. Use JSON Patch when clients must change single array elements or need a test step. A partial DTO is fine only if null never has a meaning of its own; otherwise you cannot tell "clear it" from "leave it".
Return the DTO vs return ResponseEntity vs throw an exception: how should a controller respond?

| Return DTO | Return ResponseEntity<DTO> | Throw, handled by @RestControllerAdvice
Status | 200, or fixed with @ResponseStatus | Chosen per call | Mapped once per exception type
Headers | No | Yes: Location, ETag, caching | In the handler
Best for | Simple reads | Creation, conditional requests, downloads | Not found, conflicts, validation errors
Readability | Cleanest | More verbose | Keeps error handling in one place
Rule of thumb: return plain DTOs for the happy path, ResponseEntity when you need headers or a non-200 success code, and throw domain exceptions that one advice turns into ProblemDetail. Avoid returning ResponseEntity<?> with error bodies from many places.
